Start here

How to actually use this sheet without shooting yourself in the foot

This tab is the rulebook. The single biggest way people waste months on DSA prep is skipping around — solving a flashy hard problem in a pattern they haven't earned yet, half-understanding it, and never going back to fix the gap. Follow the sequence below and that can't happen.

⚠

The one rule that matters more than any other

Never solve a Part 2 pattern problem until its Part 1 foundation module is fully done. Every pattern card in the Pattern Atlas assumes you already know the data structure it's built on. If you attempt a Tree DFS problem before finishing the Binary Trees foundation module, you'll pattern-match off someone else's code instead of reasoning from the structure — and that habit is what causes people to freeze on a slightly-different problem in an interview.

💾

Your progress saves automatically — in this browser only

Every ✓ (solved) and ★ (revise) you click is stored in this browser's local storage, tied to this file. Nothing is uploaded anywhere. That also means progress won't follow you to a different browser or device, and clearing your browser data will erase it — so keep using the same browser/file, and consider it a personal tracker rather than a synced account. Use Reset progress in the header any time you want a clean slate.

The learning loop

Repeat this for every module and every pattern

Same seven steps, every single time, whether you're on module 1 (Programming Basics) or pattern 45 (Trie: Prefix Matching). Consistency here is what turns this from a checklist into a system.

01

Read the explanation before touching a single problem

Every module and pattern card opens with a plain-English explanation and a "how to recognise it" checklist. Read both fully before you open the first linked problem. You're not allowed to code yet — you're building the mental model the code will hang on.

02

Trace the diagram and code skeleton by hand

Copy the tiny code skeleton onto paper (or a blank file) and dry-run it against the example in the diagram. If you can't predict what a variable holds after one loop iteration, you're not ready for the problems yet — re-read the explanation.

03

Solve every problem in the card, top to bottom, in order

The problems inside each card are ordered easiest-first. Do not jump to the hardest problem in a pattern to "test yourself" — the earlier problems exist to load the pattern into muscle memory before the harder ones stress-test it.

04

Time-box every attempt: struggle, then look, never guess-scroll

Give yourself 25–30 focused minutes on a problem before opening any hint or editorial. If you're stuck, re-read this pattern's explanation card first — the answer is usually in the recognition checklist you skimmed too fast. Only open TUF/LeetCode/GFG editorials after a genuine attempt.

05

Do not open a pattern until its foundation module is fully solved

Use the Prerequisite Map below. If you haven't finished the Binary Trees foundation module, the Tree BFS and Tree DFS pattern cards are off-limits — even if a problem "looks easy". Solving a pattern problem without its foundation is how bad habits and copied solutions creep in.

06

Close a module only when every problem shows a genuine, understood solve

"Solved by pasting an editorial" is not solved. Before moving to the next module, be able to re-derive each solution's core idea out loud, from memory, without looking.

07

Revisit each pattern a week later — cold, no notes

Pick 2–3 problems at random from a pattern you finished 5–7 days ago and re-solve them without looking at your old code. If you can't, that pattern isn't done — loop back before advancing further.

Sequencing

The exact order to move through this sheet

Work straight down the Foundations tab, top to bottom — the modules are already ordered by dependency (you can't do Recursion problems comfortably without Basics, can't do Backtracking without Recursion, and so on). Only after all 14 Foundation modules are done should you start the Pattern Atlas — and even then, follow the prerequisite map below rather than picking patterns at random.

  1. Foundations, in tab order — Programming Basics → Recursion → Hashing → Sorting → Arrays → Strings → Linked List → Bit Manipulation → Stack & Queue → Heaps → Binary Trees → Binary Search Trees → Graphs → Tries.
  2. Then Pattern Atlas, grouped by the structure you just learned — do the Array/String/LinkedList-based patterns first (Two Pointers → Sliding Window → Cyclic Sort → Merge Intervals → Fast & Slow → Reversal), since they reinforce what you just finished.
  3. Recursion-based patterns next — Subsets/Subsequence Pattern, then Backtracking. Don't touch these until the Recursion foundation module is solid.
  4. Structure-specific patterns — Stack/Queue patterns, Heap patterns (Top-K → K-way Merge → Two Heaps), Tree patterns (BFS → DFS → BST), Graph patterns (Traversal → Topological Sort → Shortest Path → Union-Find/MST → Advanced), Trie pattern.
  5. Dynamic Programming absolutely last. Dynamic Programming is deliberately last. Every DP pattern (Knapsack, LCS, LIS, MCM, Grid DP) is the recursion you built in the Recursion foundation and the Subsets pattern, just memoized — attempting DP before those two are solid is the #1 cause of feeling like DP is 'magic'.

Per-problem checklist

The protocol for every single problem, no exceptions

Pin this next to whatever editor you're solving in. Skipping steps here is the second most common way people fool themselves into thinking a problem is "done".

  1. Read the problem statement twice. Restate it in your own words before thinking about code.
  2. Identify the data structure(s) involved — check the Foundations tab if you're unsure what operations that structure supports.
  3. Run it through the "How to Spot a Pattern" table on the Pattern Atlas tab. Name the pattern out loud before coding.
  4. Write the recurrence / pointer movement / traversal logic in plain English or pseudocode first.
  5. Only now write real code. Trace it against the example input by hand before running it.
  6. Check edge cases: empty input, single element, all-duplicates, already-sorted, negative numbers.
  7. State the time and space complexity — if you can't, you don't fully understand the solution yet.
  8. Mark it solved only after steps 1–7. Then move to the next problem in the card, in order.
↻

Revision isn't optional

Memory fades faster than confidence does — you'll feel like you "know" a pattern days after actually forgetting the details. Every 7 days, pull 2–3 random problems from a pattern you already finished and re-solve them cold. Use the search bar (top of every tab) to jump straight back to any pattern or module for this.

Data structures, in the order you should actually learn them

01 Programming Basics & Logic Building Start here40 problems40 Easy0/40 solved ›

Before any data structure makes sense you need fluency with the raw material every solution is built from: variables, conditionals, loops, and the built-in containers (STL / Java Collections) that give you arrays, pairs, sets and maps for free. The star-pattern problems aren't decoration — they train you to translate a shape in your head into nested loops, which is the exact same muscle you use later to translate a recursion tree or a DP table into code.

  • Get comfortable with input/output and control flow before touching data structures.
  • Learn what your language's standard library already gives you (vector/list, pair, set, map) — don't reinvent them.
  • Basic maths (primes, GCD/LCM, divisors) shows up constantly inside harder problems as a sub-routine.
  • Pattern-printing = loop-control training wheels: master row/column reasoning here, reuse it everywhere.
approach.py
for i in range(n):
    for j in range(cols(i)):
        print(shape(i, j), end='')
    print()

02 Recursion Foundation14 problems9 Easy5 Medium0/14 solved ›

Recursion is a function that trusts a smaller version of itself to do the work, then combines the result. Every recursive solution has the same skeleton: a base case that stops the shrinking, and a recursive case that shrinks the input and trusts the answer will come back correct. Master this skeleton on simple problems (print numbers, reverse a string, check palindrome) before you meet backtracking or DP — they are recursion with extra bookkeeping.

  • Always identify the base case first — it's the exit door that prevents infinite recursion.
  • Trust the recursive leap: assume f(n-1) already works, then figure out how to build f(n) from it.
  • Draw the recursion tree on paper for at least 5 problems — this is what your brain will do automatically later.
  • Watch the call stack: recursion depth = space complexity, this matters for interviews.
approach.py
def solve(n):
    if n == 0:                 # base case
        return 0
    return n + solve(n - 1)    # recursive case

03 Hashing Foundation3 problems3 Easy0/3 solved ›

Hashing trades a little memory for O(1) average lookup — the single biggest lever for turning an O(n²) brute force into O(n). Anytime you catch yourself writing a nested loop to check 'does this value exist elsewhere', stop and ask if a hash-set or hash-map with a single pass would do it in O(n).

  • Frequency counting, 'have I seen this before', and 'what's the complement I need' are the three classic hashing signals.
  • A hash-map turns 'search' into 'lookup' — O(n) instead of O(n²) for pair/subarray problems.
  • Know the trade-off: hashing gives speed but no ordering — use a sorted structure/BST if order matters.
approach.py
seen = {}
for i, x in enumerate(arr):
    if target - x in seen:
        return (seen[target-x], i)
    seen[x] = i

04 Sorting Techniques Foundation7 problems7 Easy0/7 solved ›

Sorting is rarely the final answer — it's a pre-processing step that unlocks other techniques. A sorted array makes two-pointers and binary search possible; a sorted-by-start-time interval list makes greedy scheduling trivial. Learn selection/bubble/insertion for intuition, then merge sort and quick sort for the divide-and-conquer pattern that reappears in real interview problems.

  • Merge sort's 'split, solve, combine' shape is the template for many divide-and-conquer problems.
  • Quick sort's partition step reappears verbatim in the 'kth largest element' family of problems.
  • If a problem says 'array is sorted' or you sort it yourself, immediately consider two-pointers or binary search.
approach.py
def merge_sort(a):
    if len(a) <= 1: return a
    mid = len(a)//2
    L, R = merge_sort(a[:mid]), merge_sort(a[mid:])
    return merge(L, R)

05 Arrays Data Structure12 problems12 Easy0/12 solved ›

The array is the mother structure — contiguous memory, O(1) index access, O(n) search. Every pattern in Part 2 (two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums, Kadane's) is really just 'a smarter way to walk an array once instead of twice'. Get the easy problems here rock solid — they are the vocabulary the patterns are written in. Two array problems from this chapter (finding a missing number, finding a number appearing once) are deliberately held back for Part 2, where they anchor the Cyclic Sort and Bit Manipulation patterns.

  • O(1) random access is the array's superpower — use index math whenever possible.
  • Insertion/deletion in the middle is O(n) — this is why linked lists exist.
  • 'Do it in one pass' or 'without extra space' in a question is your cue that a pattern applies.
approach.py
best = arr[0]
for x in arr[1:]:
    best = max(best, x)

06 Strings Data Structure7 problems7 Easy0/7 solved ›

A string is an array of characters, so every array trick applies — plus string-specific tools like ASCII/frequency arrays, and the idea that a string reversed, or read as a palindrome-check, is just two-pointer array logic. Get comfortable with in-place vs new-string operations, since strings are immutable in many languages.

  • Strings are (mostly) immutable — repeated concatenation in a loop is an O(n²) trap, use a buffer/list + join.
  • Two-pointer (start/end) is the default approach for reversal and palindrome checks.
  • A 26-length frequency array is usually faster than a hash-map for lowercase-letter problems.
approach.py
def is_palindrome(s):
    i, j = 0, len(s)-1
    while i < j:
        if s[i] != s[j]: return False
        i += 1; j -= 1
    return True

07 Linked List Data Structure9 problems9 Easy0/9 solved ›

A linked list gives up O(1) random access in exchange for O(1) insertion/deletion anywhere, using pointers instead of contiguous memory. Nearly every linked-list interview problem is one of three moves: (1) walk two pointers at different speeds, (2) rewire next-pointers to reverse a section, or (3) use a dummy head to avoid edge-case code for the first node.

  • A dummy/sentinel head node removes 90% of 'what if the head changes' edge cases.
  • Fast & slow pointers (Floyd's) find the middle, detect cycles, and find the Nth-from-end — one trick, many uses.
  • Always draw the pointer rewiring on paper before coding a reversal — off-by-one pointer bugs are the #1 mistake.
approach.py
slow = fast = head
while fast and fast.next:
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next
# slow is now the middle node

08 Bit Manipulation Data Structure8 problems8 Easy0/8 solved ›

Every integer is already a tiny array of 0s and 1s, and bitwise operators let you touch all of them in O(1) hardware-level time. The recurring superpowers are: XOR cancels duplicates, AND/OR isolate or set specific bits, and left/right shift multiply/divide by powers of two instantly.

  • x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x → XOR is the go-to trick for 'find the unique/odd-occurring element'.
  • x & (x-1) clears the lowest set bit — used to count set bits or check power-of-two in O(1).
  • Left shift 1<<k builds a mask for the k-th bit; combine with & to test, | to set, ^ to toggle.
approach.py
def count_set_bits(x):
    c = 0
    while x:
        x &= (x - 1)   # clears lowest set bit
        c += 1
    return c

09 Stack & Queue Data Structure8 problems8 Easy0/8 solved ›

Stack (LIFO) and Queue (FIFO) are the two disciplines for temporarily holding items. A stack is your tool whenever a problem needs 'the most recent unmatched thing' — brackets, undo history, DFS. A queue is your tool whenever you need strict arrival order — BFS, task scheduling, sliding window maximums (deque).

  • Stack = LIFO: last in, first out. Perfect for matching pairs (brackets) and reversing order.
  • Queue = FIFO: first in, first out. Perfect for level-order / breadth-first processing.
  • A deque (double-ended queue) is a queue and a stack fused — used in sliding-window-maximum and monotonic-queue patterns.
approach.py
stack = []
for ch in s:
    if ch in '([{': stack.append(ch)
    elif not stack or not matches(stack.pop(), ch):
        return False
return not stack

10 Heaps Data Structure4 problems4 Easy0/4 solved ›

A heap is a tree that only promises one thing: the smallest (min-heap) or largest (max-heap) element is always at the root, retrievable in O(1) and removable in O(log n). Reach for a heap whenever a problem says 'kth largest/smallest', 'top-K', or 'always process the smallest/largest next' (priority scheduling).

  • Min-heap → quick access to the smallest element; max-heap → quick access to the largest.
  • Insert and extract are both O(log n) — much cheaper than re-sorting the whole collection every time.
  • 'Kth largest', 'merge K sorted lists', 'median of a stream' are the classic heap giveaway phrases.
approach.py
import heapq
heap = []
for x in nums:
    heapq.heappush(heap, x)
    if len(heap) > k:
        heapq.heappop(heap)   # keeps k largest
# heap[0] is the kth largest

11 Binary Trees Data Structure13 problems13 Easy0/13 solved ›

A tree is a graph with no cycles and one root — the hierarchical cousin of the linked list. Almost every tree problem is a traversal (inorder/preorder/postorder/level-order) with a tiny twist in what you do at each node. Master the four traversals cold, both recursive and iterative, and 80% of tree problems become 'which traversal + what do I track'.

  • Preorder (root-left-right) is great for copying/serializing a tree.
  • Inorder (left-root-right) on a BST visits nodes in sorted order — this is huge.
  • Postorder (left-right-root) is needed when a node's answer depends on its children's answers first (heights, diameters).
  • Level-order (BFS with a queue) is needed for anything about 'levels' or 'width' — the direct foundation for the Tree BFS pattern in Part 2.
approach.py
def inorder(node, out):
    if not node: return
    inorder(node.left, out)
    out.append(node.val)
    inorder(node.right, out)

12 Binary Search Trees Data Structure3 problems3 Easy0/3 solved ›

A BST layers the binary-search idea onto a tree shape: for every node, everything in the left subtree is smaller and everything in the right subtree is bigger. That single invariant gives you O(log n) search, insert and delete on a balanced tree, and means an inorder traversal always yields sorted output.

  • At every node you decide left-or-right exactly like binary search on an array — that's the whole algorithm.
  • Inorder traversal of a BST = sorted array, for free.
  • A skewed BST (all left or all right children) degrades to O(n) — this is why balanced trees (AVL/Red-Black) exist.
approach.py
def search(node, target):
    if not node or node.val == target: return node
    if target < node.val: return search(node.left, target)
    return search(node.right, target)

13 Graphs Data Structure6 problems6 Easy0/6 solved ›

A graph generalises a tree by allowing cycles and multiple connections — nodes (vertices) linked by edges, which may be directed or weighted. Almost the entire graph curriculum boils down to two traversal engines (BFS and DFS) applied with a different question layered on top: shortest path, connectivity, cycle detection, ordering.

  • Represent graphs as an adjacency list — adjacency matrix wastes space unless the graph is dense.
  • BFS explores level by level with a queue — it's what gives you the shortest path in an unweighted graph.
  • DFS explores as deep as possible with a stack/recursion — it's what gives you cycle detection and topological order.
  • Always ask: directed or undirected? weighted or not? — this decides which algorithm applies next.
approach.py
def bfs(start, adj):
    visited, q = {start}, deque([start])
    while q:
        node = q.popleft()
        for nxt in adj[node]:
            if nxt not in visited:
                visited.add(nxt); q.append(nxt)

14 Tries Data Structure1 problems1 Easy0/1 solved ›

A trie (prefix tree) stores strings letter by letter along tree branches, so that every string sharing a prefix shares the same path. This turns 'does any word start with this prefix' or 'autocomplete' from an O(n·k) scan into an O(k) walk down the tree, where k is the word length.

  • Each node holds up to 26 children (for lowercase English) plus an 'end of word' flag.
  • Insert and search are both O(k) where k = word length — independent of how many words are stored.
  • Reach for a trie whenever you see 'prefix', 'autocomplete', or 'dictionary of words' in a problem.
approach.py
class TrieNode:
    def __init__(self):
        self.children = {}
        self.is_end = False

def insert(root, word):
    node = root
    for ch in word:
        node = node.children.setdefault(ch, TrieNode())
    node.is_end = True

Part 2 — Learn to predict the pattern

How to spot a pattern before you even start coding

Before diving into problems, run the question through this checklist. Recognising the shape of a problem is 80% of solving it fast.

How to spot a pattern — quick reference
If you notice…Reach for…Because…
Sorted array/string, pair-sum, dedup, palindrome checkTwo PointersTwo converging indices exploit sorted order to avoid a nested loop.
'Contiguous subarray/substring' + a condition (sum, distinct chars, max/min length)Sliding WindowYou only ever need to adjust one boundary at a time instead of recomputing from scratch.
Linked list problems — cycle detection, middle node, Nth from endFast & Slow PointersTwo pointers moving at different speeds expose structure with zero extra memory.
'Reverse a list / sublist' with O(1) spaceIn-place Linked List ReversalRewiring next-pointers avoids allocating a new list entirely.
Overlapping ranges, scheduling, calendar/meeting problemsMerge IntervalsSorting by start time turns overlap-checking into one linear sweep.
Array holds numbers in a known range 1..n, find missing/duplicateCyclic SortEach value has one 'correct home' index — placing values there in one pass reveals the odd one out.
'Level-order', 'shortest path in unweighted tree/grid', tree 'views'Tree BFSBreadth-first level tracking is the only way to reason about levels/width/views correctly.
'Root-to-leaf path', tree sum/depth/diameter, backtracking on a treeTree DFSThe answer at a node depends on going all the way down first, then combining on the way back up.
'Median of a stream', 'smallest of the largest half'Two HeapsSplitting data into a max-heap (lower half) and min-heap (upper half) gives O(1) median access.
'Find all combinations / permutations / subsets'Subsets & BacktrackingYou need to explore a decision tree and undo choices that don't pan out.
Sorted or rotated array, 'minimize the max / maximize the min'Modified Binary SearchThe search space is monotonic even when the raw array or the answer range isn't obviously 'sorted'.
'Kth largest/smallest', 'top-K', frequency-based rankingTop-K ElementsA size-K heap tracks the current extreme without a full sort.
Merge K sorted lists/arraysK-way MergeA heap tracks 'who's next' across many sorted sources at once.
'Order tasks given dependencies / prerequisites'Topological SortYou need a linear order that respects directed edges — only possible on a DAG.
'Connect / group islands / friend circles / provinces'Union-Find / Graph TraversalYou're merging elements into connected components incrementally, or exploring reachability.
'Count ways to reach a state' or 'min/max cost to reach a state', overlapping sub-problemsDynamic ProgrammingThe same sub-problem recurs — cache it instead of recomputing (memoization/tabulation).
'Prefix of a word', dictionary of strings, autocompleteTrieShared prefixes should share memory and search work.

01 Two Pointers Two Pointers7 problems4 Medium3 Hard0/7 solved ›

Two indices move toward each other (or in tandem) across a sorted structure, letting you check pairs, dedupe, or partition in a single O(n) pass instead of a nested O(n²) loop. Once the array is sorted, moving the left pointer up shrinks the sum, moving the right pointer down grows it — that single lever solves the whole pair/triplet/quadruplet-sum family.

  • Sort first if the problem doesn't already guarantee order — two pointers need a monotonic structure to work correctly.
  • Pair-sum family (2Sum on sorted input, 3Sum, 4Sum): fix the earliest index/indices, then two-pointer the remaining range, skipping duplicates as you go.
  • Rearrangement problems (sort colors / Dutch flag, next permutation, rearrange by sign) swap elements in place using pointer logic instead of allocating a new array.
  • Merging two sorted arrays in-place is the same left/right convergence idea, just walking two structures instead of one.
pattern.py
l, r = 0, len(arr) - 1
while l < r:
    s = arr[l] + arr[r]
    if s == target: return (l, r)
    elif s < target: l += 1
    else: r -= 1

02 Kadane's Algorithm, Prefix Sum & Counting Kadane'sPrefix Sum10 problems10 Medium0/10 solved ›

This bucket covers the 'carry a running value forward' family: Kadane's algorithm for the best contiguous subarray (extend the current run if it helps, otherwise restart), prefix sums for O(1) range queries and 'count subarrays with sum K' via a hash-map of prefix sums seen so far, and single-pass counting tricks like Boyer-Moore voting for the majority element.

  • Kadane's rule: extend the current subarray if it helps, otherwise restart from the current element.
  • prefix[i] = prefix[i-1] + arr[i] turns range-sum queries into O(1) subtraction; store prefix sums in a hash-map to count subarrays matching a target sum in one pass.
  • Boyer-Moore voting finds a majority element in O(1) space by cancelling out non-majority votes one at a time.
  • 'Rearrange/rotate/traverse a matrix in place' (spiral order, rotate 90°, set matrix zeroes) reuses this same 'one deliberate pass, track state as you go' mindset.
pattern.py
best = cur = arr[0]
for x in arr[1:]:
    cur = max(x, cur + x)   # extend or restart
    best = max(best, cur)

03 Prefix-XOR, Inversions & Divide-and-Conquer Counting Prefix XORDivide & Conquer7 problems7 Hard0/7 solved ›

A tougher counting tier: prefix-XOR (mirrors prefix-sum, but for 'subarrays with XOR = K'), and divide-and-conquer counting problems (count inversions, reverse pairs) that piggyback on merge sort's merge step to count cross-pairs in O(n log n) instead of O(n²).

  • Prefix XOR + hash-map is the XOR twin of the prefix-sum trick — same one-pass, O(n) shape.
  • 'Count inversions' and 'reverse pairs' both hide inside a modified merge sort: count cross-boundary pairs while merging two already-sorted halves.
  • Maximum product subarray needs two running values (max AND min) because a negative number can flip the smallest product into the largest.
pattern.py
def merge_count(arr):
    if len(arr) <= 1: return arr, 0
    mid = len(arr)//2
    L, cl = merge_count(arr[:mid]); R, cr = merge_count(arr[mid:])
    merged, cross, i, j = [], 0, 0, 0
    while i < len(L) and j < len(R):
        if L[i] <= R[j]: merged.append(L[i]); i += 1
        else: merged.append(R[j]); j += 1; cross += len(L) - i
    return merged + L[i:] + R[j:], cl + cr + cross

04 Cyclic Sort Cyclic Sort2 problems1 Easy1 Hard0/2 solved ›

When an array is guaranteed to contain numbers from a known range (1..n), every value has one 'correct home': index (value - 1). Walk the array once, swapping each number into its home slot; whatever ends up out of place at the end is your missing or duplicate number — no extra memory needed.

  • The giveaway phrase is 'array contains n numbers in the range 1 to n' (or 0 to n-1) plus 'find the missing/duplicate'.
  • Swap arr[i] to its home index (arr[i]-1) repeatedly until the value at i is already correct, then move on.
  • After the sort pass, a single linear scan finds any index i where arr[i] != i+1 — that mismatch reveals the missing and/or duplicate value.
pattern.py
i = 0
while i < len(arr):
    correct = arr[i] - 1
    if arr[i] != arr[correct]:
        arr[i], arr[correct] = arr[correct], arr[i]
    else:
        i += 1
# now arr[i] should equal i+1 everywhere; scan for the mismatch

05 Merge Intervals Intervals6 problems1 Hard5 Medium/Hard0/6 solved ›

Whenever a problem hands you a list of ranges (meetings, events, intervals) and asks about overlap, merging, insertion, or how many resources you need simultaneously, sort by start time first. That single step turns any overlap-related question into one linear left-to-right sweep.

  • Sort by start time — after that, two intervals overlap only if the next one's start is before (or at) the current merged interval's end.
  • 'Insert a new interval' = walk sorted intervals, keep everything ending before the new one starts, merge everything overlapping it, keep everything starting after it ends.
  • 'Minimum platforms/meeting rooms needed' = sort arrivals and departures separately, sweep with two pointers counting how many are simultaneously active.
pattern.py
intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
merged = [intervals[0]]
for s, e in intervals[1:]:
    if s <= merged[-1][1]:
        merged[-1][1] = max(merged[-1][1], e)
    else:
        merged.append([s, e])

06 Sliding Window Sliding Window8 problems8 Medium0/8 solved ›

Whenever you need the best contiguous window (subarray/substring) satisfying a condition, grow the window's right edge to include more elements, and shrink from the left edge only when the condition breaks. This avoids the O(n²) trap of checking every possible window from scratch.

  • Fixed-size window: slide by adding the new right element and removing the old left element each step.
  • Variable-size window: grow right always; shrink left only while the window is 'invalid'.
  • Track window state (sum, char counts, distinct count) incrementally — never recompute from scratch.
pattern.py
l = 0
for r in range(len(arr)):
    window_add(arr[r])
    while window_invalid():
        window_remove(arr[l]); l += 1
    best = max(best, r - l + 1)

07 Advanced Sliding Window Sliding Window4 problems4 Hard0/4 solved ›

The hard tier combines sliding window with an auxiliary hash-map/count structure to track more complex validity conditions (minimum window containing all characters of another string, longest substring with at most K distinct characters, subarrays with exactly K distinct values via 'at most K' minus 'at most K-1').

  • 'Exactly K' is often easier as atMost(K) - atMost(K-1) — a very reusable trick.
  • Keep a frequency map alongside the window pointers to know instantly when the condition is satisfied.
  • Shrink aggressively once valid, to always test the smallest valid window at each right position.
pattern.py
def at_most_k_distinct(arr, k):
    count, l, res = {}, 0, 0
    for r, x in enumerate(arr):
        count[x] = count.get(x, 0) + 1
        while len(count) > k:
            count[arr[l]] -= 1
            if count[arr[l]] == 0: del count[arr[l]]
            l += 1
        res += r - l + 1
    return res

08 Modified Binary Search — 1D & Rotated Arrays Binary Search13 problems13 Easy0/13 solved ›

The classic pattern: on a sorted array, compare the middle element to your target and throw away the half that can't contain the answer. Variants (first/last occurrence, search in rotated sorted array, find peak element) all keep this same 'halve the search space' skeleton — only the comparison logic changes.

  • Always define lo/hi/mid consistently and be deliberate about which side you keep (lo=mid+1 vs hi=mid-1).
  • 'Rotated sorted array' still allows binary search — one half is always properly sorted, check which one.
  • 'Find first/last occurrence' = binary search that keeps narrowing even after finding a match.
pattern.py
lo, hi = 0, len(arr) - 1
while lo <= hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if arr[mid] == target: return mid
    elif arr[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
    else: hi = mid - 1
return -1

09 Modified Binary Search — On the Answer Binary Search14 problems14 Medium0/14 solved ›

Sometimes the input isn't sorted at all, but the *answer space* is monotonic — e.g. 'can I ship all packages within D days if capacity = X' is false for small X and true for large X. Binary search directly on the range of possible answers, using a helper 'is this answer feasible?' check as the comparison.

  • Ask: is there a value X such that everything below X fails and everything above X works (or vice versa)?
  • Write a feasibility/check(x) function first — the binary search loop around it barely changes between problems.
  • Common giveaway phrases: 'minimize the maximum', 'maximize the minimum', 'smallest X such that...'.
pattern.py
lo, hi = min_possible, max_possible
while lo < hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if feasible(mid):
        hi = mid          # try smaller
    else:
        lo = mid + 1
return lo

10 Modified Binary Search — 2D Matrices Binary Search5 problems5 Medium0/5 solved ›

A row-and-column sorted matrix is really a 1D sorted array in disguise — you can map a single index back to (row, col) with div/mod, or start from a corner (top-right) and eliminate a full row or column with each comparison.

  • If every row's last element < next row's first element, treat the whole matrix as one flat sorted array.
  • If only rows and columns are individually sorted, start at the top-right corner and move left/down to eliminate a line per step.
  • mid → (mid // cols, mid % cols) converts a flat index back into 2D coordinates.
pattern.py
lo, hi = 0, rows*cols - 1
while lo <= hi:
    mid = (lo+hi)//2
    val = matrix[mid//cols][mid%cols]
    if val == target: return True
    elif val < target: lo = mid+1
    else: hi = mid-1

11 String Pattern Matching & Manipulation Strings8 problems8 Medium0/8 solved ›

Medium string problems typically need a supporting structure: a frequency map for anagram-style comparisons, careful index math for string-to-integer parsing, or a stack for nested structure (repeated string decoding). Recognise which sub-tool the wording is hinting at.

  • Parsing numbers/roman numerals from strings is about careful state machines, not clever tricks.
pattern.py
from collections import Counter
def is_anagram(a, b):
    return Counter(a) == Counter(b)

12 Advanced String Matching (KMP / Z-Function) KMPZ-Function9 problems9 Hard0/9 solved ›

Naive substring search re-checks characters it has already seen, costing O(n·m). KMP precomputes a 'longest prefix that is also a suffix' (LPS) array so that on a mismatch, you jump forward using knowledge you already gathered instead of restarting. The Z-function is a close cousin that encodes, for every position, how long a match with the prefix extends.

  • Build the LPS/failure array once in O(m), then scan the text in O(n) — total O(n+m), no backtracking.
  • On a mismatch, don't reset the text pointer — use the failure array to know how much of the pattern you can safely skip.
  • Z-array[i] = length of the longest substring starting at i that matches the prefix of the string — great for multi-pattern search.
pattern.py
def build_lps(p):
    lps = [0]*len(p); k = 0
    for i in range(1, len(p)):
        while k and p[i] != p[k]: k = lps[k-1]
        if p[i] == p[k]: k += 1
        lps[i] = k
    return lps

13 Fast & Slow Pointers Two PointersCycle Detection8 problems8 Medium0/8 solved ›

Two pointers walk the same list at different speeds (typically 1 step vs 2 steps). If there's a cycle, the fast pointer eventually laps the slow one — they must meet. The same speed-difference idea locates the middle node (fast reaches the end exactly when slow reaches the middle) and the Nth-from-end node (offset one pointer by N steps first, then move both together).

  • Cycle detection: if fast ever equals slow, there's a cycle; to find the entry point, reset one pointer to head and move both one step at a time — they meet exactly at the cycle's start.
  • Middle of a list: move slow by 1 and fast by 2; when fast hits the end, slow is at the middle.
  • Nth-from-end / palindrome-check: offset one pointer first (by N, or to the middle) so the remaining walk directly gives you the answer.
pattern.py
slow = fast = head
while fast and fast.next:
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next
    if slow == fast:
        return True   # cycle detected

14 In-place Linked List Reversal Reversal9 problems7 Medium2 Hard0/9 solved ›

Reversal is pure pointer rewiring: walk the list once, and at each node flip its .next pointer to point backward instead of forward, using a 'prev' pointer to remember where to point to. Group-reversal, rotation, and list-based arithmetic (add 1 / add two numbers, which need the least-significant digit first) all build directly on this single rewiring move.

  • Always keep a 'prev' pointer when reversing — you need it to rewire the .next pointer backward.
  • 'Reverse in groups of K' = reverse a fixed-size chunk using the same iterative logic, then recursively/iteratively reconnect to the next reversed chunk.
  • 'Rotate a list' = find the new tail/head by walking (length - k) steps, then relink three pointers — no full reversal needed.
  • List arithmetic (add 1, add two numbers) is easiest after reversing so you can process from the least-significant digit like normal manual addition.
pattern.py
prev, cur = None, head
while cur:
    nxt = cur.next
    cur.next = prev
    prev = cur
    cur = nxt
return prev   # new head

15 Doubly Linked List Design Design3 problems3 Medium0/3 solved ›

A doubly linked list adds a 'prev' pointer, trading a little extra memory for O(1) removal of a known node and O(1) traversal in both directions. This is the backbone of classic 'design a data structure' interview questions like LRU Cache, where you need O(1) access AND O(1) reordering.

  • Prev + next pointers let you delete any known node in O(1) without walking from the head.
  • LRU Cache = hash-map (for O(1) lookup) + doubly linked list (for O(1) reordering of recency).
  • Always keep sentinel head/tail dummy nodes in DLL-based designs to avoid null-pointer edge cases.
pattern.py
class Node:
    def __init__(self, k, v):
        self.k, self.v = k, v
        self.prev = self.next = None
# removing `node` in O(1):
node.prev.next = node.next
node.next.prev = node.prev

16 Advanced Linked List: Merge & Randomization MergeDesign2 problems2 Hard0/2 solved ›

The remaining hard-tier problems: deep-copying a list that has extra random pointers (using a hash-map from old node → new node), and flattening a multi-level list where each node also has a 'child' sorted list attached (a repeated merge-two-sorted-lists operation).

  • Copying a list with random pointers → first pass builds old→new node mapping, second pass wires next/random using the map.
  • Flattening a multi-level list is a repeated 'merge two sorted lists' operation applied level by level.
  • Both problems reward drawing the pointer structure on paper before coding — the logic is simple but easy to mis-wire.
pattern.py
old_to_new = {}
node = head
while node:
    old_to_new[node] = Node(node.val)
    node = node.next
node = head
while node:
    old_to_new[node].next = old_to_new.get(node.next)
    old_to_new[node].random = old_to_new.get(node.random)
    node = node.next

17 Subsets / Subsequence Pattern RecursionSubsets12 problems12 Medium0/12 solved ›

The 'take it or leave it' template: at every element, branch into two recursive calls — one that includes the current element in the answer, one that skips it. This single template generates all subsets, all subsequences with a given sum, and is the direct ancestor of the 0/1 knapsack DP pattern.

  • Two branches per element: include it, or don't — 2^n total leaves in the recursion tree.
  • Add a pruning condition (e.g. 'stop if running sum already exceeds target') to cut dead branches early.
  • This exact shape becomes 0/1 Knapsack DP once you notice overlapping sub-problems and memoize.
pattern.py
def solve(i, cur):
    if i == n:
        report(cur); return
    solve(i+1, cur + [arr[i]])   # include
    solve(i+1, cur)              # exclude

18 Backtracking Pattern BacktrackingPermutations8 problems8 Hard0/8 solved ›

Backtracking is recursion with an undo step: make a choice, recurse deeper, and if that path doesn't lead anywhere valid, undo the choice before trying the next option. This is how you generate permutations, solve N-Queens/Sudoku, and find all valid combinations under constraints — you're doing a depth-first search over a tree of decisions, pruning branches that can never succeed.

  • The 3-step loop is always: choose → explore (recurse) → un-choose (backtrack).
  • Prune as early as possible — check constraint validity before recursing deeper, not after.
  • Mark/unmark visited state (a 'used[]' array, or mutate-then-revert the board) so sibling branches start clean.
pattern.py
def backtrack(path, choices):
    if is_solution(path):
        report(path); return
    for c in choices:
        if not valid(path, c): continue
        path.append(c)                 # choose
        backtrack(path, choices)       # explore
        path.pop()                     # un-choose

Bit Manipulation Patterns

11 problems · 2 patterns

19 Bit Manipulation Tricks Bit TricksXOR6 problems1 Easy5 Medium0/6 solved ›

Beyond the basics, interview bit-tricks combine XOR/AND/shift into small formulas that replace loops entirely: XOR cancels every number that appears an even number of times, leaving only the odd-one-out — this single idea solves 'find the unique element' and, with one extra partitioning step, 'find the two unique elements' too.

  • x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x → XOR-ing the whole array cancels every paired value, leaving only the number that appears once.
  • Partition-by-XOR: XOR all numbers, find any set bit in the result, split the array by that bit to isolate two unique numbers.
  • 'Count total set bits from 1 to N' has an O(log N) closed-form pattern based on powers of two.
pattern.py
xor_all = 0
for x in nums: xor_all ^= x
diff_bit = xor_all & (-xor_all)   # lowest set bit where the two uniques differ
a = b = 0
for x in nums:
    if x & diff_bit: a ^= x
    else: b ^= x

20 Number Theory Patterns MathsExponentiation5 problems5 Medium0/5 solved ›

Fast exponentiation (binary exponentiation), computing power/roots without brute-force multiplication loops. The trick: any exponent can be written in binary, so you can compute x^n in O(log n) by repeated squaring instead of O(n) repeated multiplication.

  • x^n = (x^2)^(n/2) if n is even, x * x^(n-1) if odd — halves the work at every step.
  • This 'binary exponentiation' shape reappears in matrix exponentiation for fast Fibonacci and similar recurrences.
  • Watch for overflow/modulo requirements — take % MOD at every multiplication in competitive problems.
pattern.py
def power(x, n):
    result = 1
    while n:
        if n & 1: result *= x
        x *= x
        n >>= 1
    return result

21 Expression Conversion & Evaluation Stack6 problems6 Medium0/6 solved ›

Converting between infix (a+b), prefix (+ab) and postfix (ab+) notations, and evaluating them, all use the same tool: a stack that holds operands or partial results while you scan the expression, applying operators the moment enough operands are available.

  • Postfix evaluation: push numbers, and when you see an operator, pop two operands, apply it, push the result back.
  • Infix-to-postfix (Shunting Yard idea): use a stack to hold operators, popping to output whenever precedence allows.
  • This is a direct real-world use of stacks — it's literally how calculators and compilers parse expressions.
pattern.py
stack = []
for tok in postfix.split():
    if tok.isdigit(): stack.append(int(tok))
    else:
        b, a = stack.pop(), stack.pop()
        stack.append(apply(tok, a, b))
return stack[0]

22 Monotonic Stack / Queue Pattern Monotonic Stack11 problems11 Medium0/11 solved ›

A monotonic stack keeps its elements strictly increasing or decreasing by popping anything that violates the order before pushing a new element. This lets you answer 'nearest greater/smaller element to the left/right' for every element in a single O(n) pass, instead of an O(n²) nested-loop scan.

  • Scanning left→right with a decreasing stack finds 'next greater element' for each item in O(n) total.
  • Every element is pushed once and popped at most once — that's why it's O(n) despite the nested-looking while loop.
  • Histogram/rectangle problems (largest rectangle in histogram) use this to find, per bar, how far it can extend.
pattern.py
stack = []          # indices, decreasing height
next_greater = [-1]*n
for i, h in enumerate(heights):
    while stack and heights[stack[-1]] < h:
        next_greater[stack.pop()] = i
    stack.append(i)

23 Stack & Queue Design Pattern Design5 problems5 Medium0/5 solved ›

Implementation problems test whether you understand a structure well enough to build it from a different one, or to add extra tracking on the side: a stack that also returns the minimum in O(1) by keeping a parallel 'min-so-far' stack, a sliding-window-maximum answered with a monotonic deque, or classic system-design-flavoured caches (LRU/LFU).

  • Sliding window maximum: keep a deque of indices with decreasing values — the front is always the current window's max.
  • Min-stack: push (value, min-so-far) pairs, or maintain a secondary stack that only pushes new minimums.
  • LRU/LFU cache design is really 'pick the right combination of hash-map + linked-list/heap for O(1) operations' — see the Doubly Linked List Design pattern for the LRU half.
pattern.py
class MinStack:
    def __init__(self):
        self.st = []   # each item: (val, min_so_far)
    def push(self, x):
        m = min(x, self.st[-1][1]) if self.st else x
        self.st.append((x, m))
    def get_min(self):
        return self.st[-1][1]

Heap Patterns

13 problems · 3 patterns

24 Top-K Elements Pattern HeapTop-K8 problems5 Medium3 Hard0/8 solved ›

Whenever you need the K largest/smallest/most-frequent items from a stream or collection, keep a heap of size K rather than sorting everything. For 'K largest', use a min-heap of size K — the root is always your weakest member of the top-K club, and gets evicted the moment something better arrives. Simulation problems that repeatedly grab the current smallest/largest (task scheduling, combining ropes) use the exact same heap discipline.

  • 'K largest' → min-heap of size K (root = smallest of your current top-K, evict it if a bigger element shows up).
  • 'K smallest' → max-heap of size K, same idea flipped.
  • Frequency-ranking problems (K most frequent) count first with a hash-map, then heap on the counts instead of the raw values.
  • Total cost is O(n log K), much better than O(n log n) full sort when K is small.
pattern.py
import heapq
heap = []
for x in nums:
    heapq.heappush(heap, x)
    if len(heap) > k: heapq.heappop(heap)
return heap[0]   # kth largest

25 K-way Merge Pattern HeapMerge3 problems2 Medium1 Hard0/3 solved ›

K-way merge uses a single heap to always pull the smallest 'next candidate' across K sorted sources — the multi-source generalisation of merging two sorted lists. Push the current head of each source into the heap; whichever comes out smallest gets appended to the result, and its source's next element goes back into the heap.

  • Push one representative element per source into the heap, tagged with which source it came from.
  • Pop the smallest, append it to the output, then push that source's next element (if any) back in.
  • A social-feed 'merge every followee's posts by time' problem is K-way merge wearing a different costume.
pattern.py
import heapq
heap = [(node.val, i, node) for i, node in enumerate(heads) if node]
heapq.heapify(heap)
# pop smallest, push its .next, repeat

26 Two Heaps Pattern HeapMedian2 problems2 Hard0/2 solved ›

Two-heaps splits a data stream into a max-heap for the smaller half and a min-heap for the larger half, so the median is always at the top of one of them (O(log n) insert, O(1) median lookup). The same 'balance two heaps' idea generalises to any 'best pairing across two sorted collections' problem.

  • Median-of-stream: keep the two halves balanced in size (differ by at most 1) after every insert.
  • If the max-heap (lower half) ever gets smaller/larger than the min-heap by more than 1, rebalance by popping across.
  • Whenever a problem needs 'the boundary value between a lower and upper group that keeps changing', reach for two heaps before a full re-sort.
pattern.py
# median of stream: lo = max-heap (negated), hi = min-heap
heapq.heappush(lo, -x)
heapq.heappush(hi, -heapq.heappop(lo))
if len(hi) > len(lo):
    heapq.heappush(lo, -heapq.heappop(hi))

Greedy Patterns

11 problems · 2 patterns

27 Greedy: Foundations Greedy5 problems5 Easy0/5 solved ›

The introductory greedy shape: sort by some criterion (finish time, ratio, value) and then make the locally-obvious best choice at each step without ever reconsidering it. (Interval-scheduling greedy problems — activity selection, minimum platforms, job sequencing with deadlines — now live in the Merge Intervals pattern, since they share that same sort-by-time backbone.)

  • Sort first — greedy almost never works on unsorted input because 'the best local choice' needs a clear ordering.
  • Fractional Knapsack: sort by value/weight ratio, greedily fill capacity with the highest-ratio items first.
  • If greedy 'almost' works but fails an edge case, that's usually a sign you actually need DP.
pattern.py
items.sort(key=lambda it: it.value / it.weight, reverse=True)
for it in items:
    take = min(it.weight, remaining_capacity)
    total_value += take * (it.value / it.weight)
    remaining_capacity -= take

28 Greedy: Advanced Optimization Greedy6 problems6 Medium/Hard0/6 solved ›

Harder greedy problems (job sequencing with deadlines, candy distribution, jump game reachability) require picking the right sorting key and sometimes a supporting structure or a second pass to make the greedy choice actually correct.

  • Two-pass greedy: some problems need one left-to-right pass and one right-to-left pass, taking the max/min of both (e.g. candy distribution).
  • Job sequencing with deadlines: sort by profit descending, greedily place each job in the latest free slot before its deadline.
  • Jump Game family: greedily track the farthest index reachable so far as you scan left to right — no need to try every path.
pattern.py
jobs.sort(key=lambda j: -j.profit)
slots = [False]*max_deadline
for j in jobs:
    for t in range(min(max_deadline, j.deadline)-1, -1, -1):
        if not slots[t]:
            slots[t] = True; profit += j.profit; break

Tree Patterns

29 Tree BFS Pattern BFSLevel Order8 problems5 Medium3 Hard0/8 solved ›

Tree BFS explores level by level using a queue, usually carrying a little extra state alongside each node (its horizontal distance from the root, or its depth) so you can group, compare, or spread outward correctly. Views (top/bottom/left/right), zigzag order, vertical order, and maximum width are all this exact same 'BFS with coordinates' idea; 'burn the tree' / 'nodes at distance K' are multi-source BFS starting from a specific node instead of the root.

  • Track (row, column) coordinates during BFS to solve top/bottom/left/right view and vertical order problems uniformly.
  • Zigzag traversal is level-order BFS that simply reverses the output on every other level.
  • 'Nodes at distance K' / 'burn the tree' need an undirected view of the tree (also linking child→parent) before BFS spreads outward from the target node.
pattern.py
from collections import deque
q = deque([(root, 0)])
levels = []
while q:
    size = len(q)
    level = []
    for _ in range(size):
        node, col = q.popleft()
        level.append((node.val, col))
        if node.left: q.append((node.left, col-1))
        if node.right: q.append((node.right, col+1))
    levels.append(level)

30 Tree DFS Pattern DFSRecursion18 problems7 Medium11 Hard0/18 solved ›

Tree DFS goes all the way down before combining results on the way back up (postorder-style), which is exactly what you need whenever a node's answer depends on its children's answers first: height, diameter, max path sum, and identical/symmetric checks. Root-to-leaf paths and LCA use the same depth-first descent, just tracking a path or searching both subtrees instead of combining numeric results. Tree (de)serialization and construction-from-traversal problems are DFS in the other direction — rebuilding structure from an ordered sequence.

  • 'Diameter', 'max path sum', 'height' all need postorder — compute children's answers before combining at the parent.
  • LCA: recurse into both children; if both return non-null, the current node is the LCA; otherwise pass up whichever side is non-null.
  • Keep a running/global 'best answer' variable alongside a per-call 'contribution to parent' return value — these are usually different things.
  • To rebuild a tree: preorder's first element is always the current root; find that value's index in inorder to split left/right subtrees.
pattern.py
def lca(node, p, q):
    if not node or node == p or node == q: return node
    L = lca(node.left, p, q)
    R = lca(node.right, p, q)
    if L and R: return node
    return L or R

31 BST Search & Validation Pattern BST13 problems11 Medium2 Hard0/13 solved ›

Practice problems on BSTs lean on the ordering invariant: validating a BST means checking every node falls within a (min, max) range inherited from its ancestors; finding the kth smallest is just an inorder traversal stopped early; floor/ceiling search is binary search that remembers the 'closest so far' as it walks down.

  • Validate BST by passing down a (low, high) bound to each recursive call, tightening it at every step.
  • 'Kth smallest' = inorder traversal, stop counting at K — no need to traverse the whole tree.
  • Floor/ceiling: walk down like binary search, but remember the best candidate seen before moving away from it.
pattern.py
def is_valid(node, low=float('-inf'), high=float('inf')):
    if not node: return True
    if not (low < node.val < high): return False
    return is_valid(node.left, low, node.val) and is_valid(node.right, node.val, high)

32 Graph Traversal Pattern (BFS/DFS) BFSDFS14 problems14 Medium0/14 solved ›

Most 'exploration' graph problems are BFS or DFS with a tiny twist: counting connected components (run DFS from every unvisited node), flood fill (DFS/BFS on a grid), rotting oranges (multi-source BFS starting from all rotten cells at once), or word-ladder style shortest transformation (BFS on an implicit graph of word states).

  • Multi-source BFS: push ALL starting points into the queue before the first pop — gives correct simultaneous spreading.
  • Grid problems are graphs where each cell is a node connected to its (up to 4 or 8) neighbours.
  • 'Count islands/provinces/components' = loop over all nodes, DFS/BFS from each unvisited one, increment a counter.
pattern.py
def num_islands(grid):
    count = 0
    for r in range(rows):
        for c in range(cols):
            if grid[r][c] == 1:
                count += 1
                dfs(grid, r, c)   # sink the whole island
    return count

33 Topological Sort Pattern Topo Sort7 problems7 Medium0/7 solved ›

On a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), topological sort produces a linear order where every edge u→v places u before v — exactly what you need for task scheduling with prerequisites. Kahn's algorithm (BFS using in-degree counts) and DFS-with-a-stack are the two standard implementations.

  • Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly remove nodes with in-degree 0, decrementing their neighbours' in-degree, queue newly-zero nodes.
  • DFS version: run DFS, push a node to a stack only after all its descendants are processed, then reverse the stack.
  • If you can't produce an order including every node, the graph has a cycle — this is also a cycle-detection technique.
pattern.py
indeg = compute_indegrees(graph)
q = deque([n for n in graph if indeg[n] == 0])
order = []
while q:
    n = q.popleft(); order.append(n)
    for nxt in graph[n]:
        indeg[nxt] -= 1
        if indeg[nxt] == 0: q.append(nxt)

34 Shortest Path Pattern DijkstraBellman-Ford12 problems12 Medium0/12 solved ›

Unweighted graph → plain BFS. Non-negative weighted graph → Dijkstra (a heap-driven BFS that always expands the currently-closest unvisited node). Graph with possible negative weights → Bellman-Ford (relax every edge V-1 times). All-pairs shortest paths on a small graph → Floyd-Warshall (try every node as an intermediate stop).

  • Dijkstra: pop the closest node from a min-heap, relax its neighbours' distances, push improvements — never revisit a finalized node.
  • Bellman-Ford handles negative weights and can detect negative cycles (an extra relaxation pass still improves something).
  • Floyd-Warshall's triple loop (for k, for i, for j) tries routing every pair through every possible intermediate node — O(V³) but simple.
pattern.py
dist = {start: 0}
heap = [(0, start)]
while heap:
    d, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
    if d > dist.get(u, inf): continue
    for v, w in adj[u]:
        if d + w < dist.get(v, inf):
            dist[v] = d + w
            heapq.heappush(heap, (d+w, v))

35 Union-Find & Minimum Spanning Tree MSTUnion-Find11 problems11 Medium0/11 solved ›

An MST connects every node with the minimum total edge weight and no cycles. Kruskal's algorithm sorts all edges by weight and greedily adds each one unless it would form a cycle — checked instantly using a Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find) structure with path compression and union by rank. Union-Find alone (without the MST framing) also directly answers 'are these two nodes connected' and 'how many connected components/islands/provinces are there'.

  • Kruskal's: sort edges by weight, add each edge only if its two endpoints are in different DSU components (union them after).
  • Prim's is the alternative: grow the MST one node at a time, always adding the cheapest edge leaving the current tree (heap-driven).
  • Union-Find with path compression + union by rank gives near-O(1) find/union — essential for 'are these connected' style queries too.
pattern.py
def find(x):
    if parent[x] != x: parent[x] = find(parent[x])  # path compression
    return parent[x]
def union(a, b):
    ra, rb = find(a), find(b)
    if ra != rb: parent[ra] = rb

36 Advanced Graph Algorithms (Bridges / SCC) BridgesSCC3 problems3 Hard0/3 solved ›

Bridges and articulation points (Tarjan's algorithm) find edges/nodes whose removal disconnects the graph, using a DFS that tracks discovery time and the lowest reachable ancestor time for each node. Strongly Connected Components group nodes that can all reach each other in a directed graph (Kosaraju's / Tarjan's SCC).

  • A bridge exists between u and its DFS child v when low[v] > disc[u] — v cannot reach back to u or above without that edge.
  • Kosaraju's SCC: DFS once for finish-order, reverse all edges, DFS again in finish-order to peel off SCCs one at a time.
  • These are advanced/rare-in-interviews but common in competitive programming — recognise the discovery-time/low-link vocabulary.
pattern.py
def dfs(u, parent):
    disc[u] = low[u] = timer[0]; timer[0] += 1
    for v in adj[u]:
        if disc[v] == -1:
            dfs(v, u)
            low[u] = min(low[u], low[v])
            if low[v] > disc[u]: bridges.append((u, v))
        elif v != parent:
            low[u] = min(low[u], disc[v])

37 DP Pattern: 1D / Fibonacci Style DP1D5 problems5 Medium0/5 solved ›

The gateway DP pattern: dp[i] depends on a small fixed number of earlier states, like dp[i-1] and dp[i-2] (Fibonacci, climbing stairs, house robber). Always start by writing the brute-force recursion, identify the repeated sub-calls, then convert to memoization (top-down) or tabulation (bottom-up).

  • Write the recurrence in plain English first: 'the answer for i depends on the answer for i-1 and/or i-2'.
  • Memoization = recursion + a cache dict/array; tabulation = an iterative loop filling the same array bottom-up.
  • Once tabulation works, check if you only ever need the last 1-2 values — if so, drop the array for O(1) space.
pattern.py
dp = [0]*(n+1)
dp[0], dp[1] = 0, 1
for i in range(2, n+1):
    dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]
return dp[n]

38 DP Pattern: Grid Paths DPGrid7 problems7 Medium0/7 solved ›

Grid DP problems (unique paths, minimum path sum, cherry pickup) define dp[r][c] as the best answer reachable at cell (r, c), built from the cells you could have arrived from (usually above and left). 3D variants add a third dimension for a second traveler or an extra state like 'obstacles remaining'.

  • dp[r][c] = combine(dp[r-1][c], dp[r][c-1]) is the standard 2D grid recurrence — draw the grid and mark dependencies.
  • Initialize the first row and first column separately — they only have one possible direction of arrival.
  • 3D DP (two travelers on a grid simultaneously) just adds a second (row,col) pair as extra dimensions of the same idea.
pattern.py
dp = [[0]*cols for _ in range(rows)]
dp[0][0] = grid[0][0]
for r in range(rows):
    for c in range(cols):
        if r==0 and c==0: continue
        best = min(dp[r-1][c] if r>0 else inf, dp[r][c-1] if c>0 else inf)
        dp[r][c] = grid[r][c] + best

39 DP Pattern: 0/1 Knapsack & Subsequences DPKnapsack11 problems11 Medium0/11 solved ›

This is the recursion 'include or exclude' template from the Subsets pattern, memoized. dp[i][target] = can/how-many ways can items 0..i reach 'target' by choosing to include or skip each one. Subset-sum, partition-equal-subset-sum, and target-sum problems are all this exact same table shape.

  • State is almost always (index, remaining target/capacity) — draw the 2D table with index as rows, target as columns.
  • Recurrence: dp[i][t] = dp[i-1][t] (exclude) OR dp[i-1][t-arr[i]] (include, if arr[i] <= t).
  • 'Unbounded knapsack' variant (coin change) allows reusing the same item — change the include-transition to stay on row i instead of i-1.
pattern.py
dp = [[False]*(target+1) for _ in range(n+1)]
for i in range(n+1): dp[i][0] = True
for i in range(1, n+1):
    for t in range(1, target+1):
        dp[i][t] = dp[i-1][t] or (t>=arr[i-1] and dp[i-1][t-arr[i-1]])

40 DP Pattern: LCS / String Matching DPLCS10 problems10 Medium0/10 solved ›

Two-string DP problems (Longest Common Subsequence, edit distance, wildcard matching) build a 2D table where dp[i][j] represents the answer using the first i characters of string A and first j characters of string B, with the recurrence branching on whether A[i-1] == B[j-1].

  • Match case (A[i-1]==B[j-1]): usually dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1] (extend the match diagonally).
  • Mismatch case: try skipping a character from A, from B, or both — take whichever combination the problem calls for (max/min/sum).
  • Edit distance = LCS's cousin: mismatch allows insert/delete/replace, each mapping to a specific neighbour cell (left/up/diagonal).
pattern.py
dp = [[0]*(m+1) for _ in range(n+1)]
for i in range(1, n+1):
    for j in range(1, m+1):
        if A[i-1] == B[j-1]:
            dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]
        else:
            dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])

41 DP Pattern: Buy & Sell Stocks DPGreedy6 problems6 Medium0/6 solved ›

Every stock problem tracks two running states as you scan prices left to right: the best profit if you currently HOLD a share, and the best profit if you currently DON'T hold one. Variants add a transaction-count limit, a cooldown day, or a transaction fee as extra dimensions/adjustments to this same core state machine.

  • Two states per day: hold[i] (max profit while holding a share) and free[i] (max profit while not holding).
  • hold[i] = max(hold[i-1], free[i-1] - price[i]); free[i] = max(free[i-1], hold[i-1] + price[i]).
  • 'At most K transactions' just adds a k-dimension to the same two states; 'cooldown' adds a one-day delay before re-buying.
pattern.py
hold, free = float('-inf'), 0
for price in prices:
    hold = max(hold, free - price)
    free = max(free, hold + price)
return free

42 DP Pattern: Longest Increasing Subsequence DPLIS7 problems7 Medium0/7 solved ›

dp[i] = length of the longest increasing subsequence ENDING at index i, built by checking every earlier index j where arr[j] < arr[i]. The O(n log n) upgrade replaces the O(n²) inner loop with binary search into a 'smallest tail for each length' array.

  • O(n²) version: dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j] for j < i if arr[j] < arr[i]) — simple but slow for large inputs.
  • O(n log n) version: maintain a 'tails' array; binary search for where arr[i] fits, replacing or extending — the tails array itself isn't the LIS, only its length is guaranteed correct.
  • Longest Bitonic Subsequence / Chain of Pairs are LIS in disguise — spot the 'increasing chain' shape underneath the wording.
pattern.py
import bisect
tails = []
for x in arr:
    i = bisect.bisect_left(tails, x)
    if i == len(tails): tails.append(x)
    else: tails[i] = x
return len(tails)

43 DP Pattern: Partition / MCM (Interval DP) DPInterval7 problems7 Hard0/7 solved ›

Matrix Chain Multiplication style problems ask 'where do I place the split point in this range to optimize the result' — dp[i][j] represents the best answer for the sub-range (i, j), computed by trying every possible partition point k between i and j and combining the two halves' pre-computed answers.

  • State is a RANGE (i, j), not a single index — this is the tell-tale sign of interval/partition DP.
  • Recurrence: dp[i][j] = min/max over all k in (i, j) of combine(dp[i][k], dp[k][j], cost(i,k,j)).
  • Fill the table by increasing range length (small ranges first) since dp[i][j] depends on smaller sub-ranges inside it.
pattern.py
for length in range(2, n):
    for i in range(1, n-length+1):
        j = i + length - 1
        dp[i][j] = min(
            dp[i][k] + dp[k][j] + cost(i,k,j)
            for k in range(i, j)
        )

44 DP Pattern: Maximal Square (Grid DP) DPGrid2 problems2 Hard0/2 solved ›

dp[r][c] = the side-length of the largest all-1s square whose bottom-right corner is at (r, c). It can only be as big as the smallest of the square possible above, to the left, and diagonally above-left, plus one — a single extra idea layered on top of ordinary grid DP.

  • dp[r][c] = 0 immediately if grid[r][c] == 0 — a square can't have a 0 anywhere on its bottom-right corner.
  • Otherwise dp[r][c] = 1 + min(dp[r-1][c], dp[r][c-1], dp[r-1][c-1]) — the tightest of the three neighbours caps the square size.
  • Track the running maximum of dp[r][c] across the whole grid — that's your final answer, not the last cell computed.
pattern.py
dp[r][c] = 0 if grid[r][c]=='0' else 1 + min(
    dp[r-1][c], dp[r][c-1], dp[r-1][c-1]
) if r>0 and c>0 else int(grid[r][c])
best = max(best, dp[r][c])

45 Trie: Prefix Matching Pattern Trie6 problems3 Medium3 Hard0/6 solved ›

Beyond simple insert/search, tries power prefix-counting ('how many words start with this prefix' — store a counter at each node), and the XOR-trie trick for 'maximum XOR pair' problems (insert every number's binary representation, then greedily walk the opposite bit at each level to maximize XOR).

  • Store a small counter at each trie node to answer 'how many inserted words pass through here' in O(k) per query.
  • Maximum XOR pair: insert numbers bit-by-bit (MSB first) into a binary trie, then for each number greedily prefer the opposite bit at every level.
  • A trie trades memory for guaranteed O(k) operations independent of how many strings/numbers are stored — worth it when k is small and lookups are frequent.
pattern.py
def max_xor_pair(nums):
    root = TrieNode()
    for x in nums: insert_bits(root, x)
    best = 0
    for x in nums:
        best = max(best, query_max_xor(root, x))
    return best

Before the interview

Your revision list — essentials first, your picks after

This tab opens with a predefined Essential list — the first and last problem from every one of the 45 patterns, hand-picked as the minimum you should be able to solve cold before any interview. Anything you additionally ★ star in Foundations or Pattern Atlas gets appended below it under Your Added Questions, as your own personal preference layer on top.

★

How to use this tab before an interview

  1. Start with the Essential list below — it's already built for you, one representative easy-end and hard-end problem per pattern, covering all 45 patterns automatically.
  2. Star anything extra in Foundations/Patterns that gave you trouble — problems that took multiple attempts, needed a hint, or exposed a pattern you're still shaky on. These show up under "Your Added Questions" beneath the essentials.
  3. About a week out, work through both sections cold — timed, no old notes, no editorials open. Budget roughly 20–25 minutes for a Medium and 35–40 for a Hard.
  4. Check off (✓ solved) anything you clear cleanly. Your added stars can be removed once solved twice in a row; the Essential list stays as your permanent baseline check.
  5. 1–2 days before, do a final pass on whatever's still unsolved in either section, tackled in random pattern order to simulate the unpredictability of a real interview.
  6. Zero unsolved items in both sections 24 hours before the interview is the goal.
